title: Words like gems
hookLine: a stranger writes down Manikkavasagar's songs at Chidambaram, and they open with Shiva's name
carry: talk itself becomes japa: katha japah
tomorrow: the gods are terrified of an archer born of anger. what do they offer him?

lines: A STRANGER WRITES THE SONGS DOWN.
SIGNED: THE LORD OF THE SACRED HALL.
cards: Years after the tree and the flood, Manikkavasagar has walked from temple to temple, singing. He comes at last to Chidambaram, the city of the dancing Shiva.
There, tradition says, a stranger asks him to recite all his songs, and writes them down on palm leaves as he speaks.
The next morning the bundle is found on the temple step, signed: written by the Lord of the sacred hall. The stranger was Shiva. And the songs open with five syllables: namachivaya.

teach.b: The book is the Tiruvachakam, the sacred utterance, and Tamil Shaivas still sing it in homes and temples. Its first song opens namachivaya vazhga: long live namah shivaya, the five-syllable mantra.
When the priests asked what the songs meant, tradition says Manikkavasagar pointed to the dancing Shiva, walked into the shrine, and was not seen again. The meaning was him.
That mantra is the heart of a practice called japa: repeating a divine name, slowly, with attention, often on a string of a hundred and eight beads.

teach.h: JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Om namah shivaya, again and again, until the name is the groove the mind runs in.
Now the Shiva Sutras, in the book's last section: katha japah. Katha is talk, conversation. For the awakened yogi, his conversation is japa.
Commentators explain: japa keeps awareness of Shiva alive, again and again. For someone who rests in that awareness all the time, there's nothing left to switch on.

The lines around it say the same of the body, keeping it going is the vow, and of giving: the gift is knowledge of the self. That's how a poet's spoken words could become scripture: they already carried the name.
And it's why so many Hindus greet each other with a god's name, Ram Ram, Jai Shri Krishna, Har Har Mahadev, and murmur Shiva, Shiva while they cook. Not every word is holy yet.
The practice is to say the name so often that, one day, the talk itself is japa.

how: Japa is a Hindu practice: repeating a mantra or divine name, often counted on a mala of 108 beads; Tamil Shaivas sing Manikkavasagar's Tiruvachakam in homes and temples, and many Hindus greet each other with a god's name.

o: a sutra telling the awakened yogi to stop talking
a sutra saying that for the awakened, ordinary talk is japa
a sutra saying only chanting in a temple counts

games.q: the name, again and again — tap the pairs.

s: the Tiruvachakam's first song opens with namachivaya
namachivaya vazhga: long live namah shivaya.
the Shiva Sutras say the awakened yogi stops talking
they say his conversation is japa.
japa only counts with beads, in a temple
beads help, but many Hindus say the name while working, cooking, walking.

games.q: your grandmother says Shiva's name under her breath all day while she works. in today's teaching, what is that?
games.why: japa is repeating the name. katha japah: for one soaked in Shiva, even talk becomes japa.

practice: Try japa the way it's done. Hold a mala if you have one, or count on the joints of your fingers, and say Om namah shivaya, softly or silently, eleven times, slowly enough to hear each syllable.
Then let an ordinary thought come, and notice whether the name is still humming under it. If you don't pray, say the meaning instead: I bow to the auspicious one.

wordCard.voice: Katha japah. His conversation is japa: for one who rests in Shiva, ordinary talk already carries the name. That closes our time in the Shiva Sutras.

orig.note: Sanskrit: katha japah, his conversation is japa.

carryVoice: Your line: talk itself becomes japa, katha japah. Say the name until it hums under everything. Rest well.
